Mountain whitefish (Prosopium williamsoni) hatch from demersal, adhesive eggs that are deposited over gravel substrates in late autumn. Upon eclosion, the yolk-sac larva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during a lecithotrophic phase that lasts several weeks. The wet weight at birth for this species is approximately 0.0048 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0048 grams], a value derived from an egg diameter of roughly 2.1 millimeters. This minute starting mass places newly emerged alevins among the smallest of the coregonine larvae, a characteristic that may influence early-life survival in the swift, cold rivers they inhabit. The incubation period itself is strongly temperature-dependent; under the stable thermal regime of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], development proceeds at a predictable pace, though hatching success can be reduced if autumn floods scour the redds. Following yolk-sac resorption, the larvae must rapidly locate productive drift-feeding stations to sustain their initial growth, as their small size and limited energy stores constrain their ability to withstand even brief periods of food deprivation.

As individuals transition into the juvenile stage, they begin exogenous feeding on aquatic insect larvae and begin to disperse from natal rearing areas. The onset of gonadal maturation in Mountain whitefish occurs at a surprisingly modest size, with puberty typically attained when individuals reach a total length of 30 centimeters [Lp = 30 centimeters]. This length at puberty corresponds to a wet weight of approximately 249.5 grams [Wwp = approximately 249.5 grams], as estimated from length-weight regressions developed for the species. Such relatively early maturation is a common life-history strategy among iteroparous salmonids inhabiting unpredictable environments, where the ability to reproduce before encountering a potentially lethal disturbance may confer a selective advantage. The transition from a feeding juvenile to a reproductively viable organism involves substantial changes in physiology and behavior, including the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and the onset of vitellogenesis in females. In many populations, males may mature at slightly smaller sizes than females, a pattern that likely reflects differing energetic costs associated with gamete production and spawning behavior.

Spawning adults of Mountain whitefish exhibit a distinct pattern of reproductive allocation that is tightly linked to seasonal thermal regimes. Under the cold-water conditions typical of their native range, held at a constant 7 °C [T = 7 °C], observations indicate that reproductively active females produce approximately 66 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 66 eggs per spawning event] and may complete approximately 365 spawning events each year [F_R_i = approximately 365 spawning events each year]. This very high fecundity leads to a daily reproduction rate of approximately 66 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 66 eggs per day], a figure that highlights the species' considerable reproductive potential. This moderate fecundity per spawning event is balanced by relatively large egg diameters, producing offspring with substantial yolk reserves that enhance early survival. As iteroparous spawners, adults can reproduce across multiple seasons, though annual reproductive effort may vary with maternal condition and prey availability. The spawning run itself is a synchronized autumnal event, during which mature teleosts migrate upstream to suitable gravel beds. Gravid females are easily identified by their distended abdomens, while males develop a slight nuptial coloration and a more streamlined body form.

The ultimate total length attained by Mountain whitefish reaches 70 centimeters [Li = 70 centimeters] in the largest documented individuals, placing this species among the more sizable members of the genus Prosopium. Such a maximum length corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of roughly 3,690 grams [Wwi = roughly 3,690 grams], a figure derived from empirical growth models that describe the allometric relationship between length and mass in this species. Individuals achieving this size are typically females in northern populations, where cooler temperatures and lower metabolic demands may permit extended somatic growth over a longer lifespan. The trade-off between rapid early growth and ultimate size is evident: populations experiencing higher mortality rates tend to mature earlier and at smaller sizes, while those in more stable environments allocate more energy to continued somatic expansion. This length-weight relationship aligns closely with that reported for the congeneric round whitefish, suggesting a conserved Bauplan within the genus. Maximum sizes are rarely observed in heavily exploited populations, where size-selective harvest truncates the age structure.

Longevity records for Prosopium williamsoni indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 17 years [am = approximately 17 years] in populations inhabiting undisturbed, cold-water habitats maintained at 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. This extended lifespan is notable among coregonines and reflects a life-history strategy characterized by slow growth, delayed senescence, and repeated reproductive events across decades. The physiological basis of this longevity likely involves low metabolic rates at cold temperatures and efficient antioxidant defenses that mitigate oxidative damage over time. Age determination using otoliths reveals that growth increments narrow considerably after sexual maturity, with most somatic expansion occurring during the first five to seven years. Older individuals often exhibit signs of reproductive senescence, including reduced fecundity and lower egg viability, though some females continue to spawn successfully well into their second decade. The interplay between temperature and lifespan is critical: at warmer thermal regimes, metabolic acceleration shortens the maximum achievable age, whereas the sustained cold of northern lakes and rivers appears to extend it.
